item.title: Record tax haul
item.description: The Fiji Revenue and Customs Service (FRCS) has reaped a historic $3.510 billion in net revenue for the financial year ending July 31, 2026, marking the highest annual collection in the institution’s history. The result is $136.2 million (4.0 per cent) above the Government’s annual forecast of $3.374b; and $25.8m (0.7 per cent) higher than the $3.485b collected in the previous financial year.
item.content:encoded:
The Fiji Revenue and Customs Service (FRCS) has reaped a historic $3.510 billion in net revenue for the financial year ending July 31, 2026, marking the highest annual collection in the institution’s history.

The result is $136.2 million (4.0 per cent) above the Government’s annual forecast of $3.374b; and $25.8m (0.7 per cent) higher than the $3.485b collected in the previous financial year.

According to the FRCS, growth was led by net income tax, which increased by $53.7m, net customs collection that increased by $46.6m, and departure tax that increased by $43.7m.

Within those categories, PAYE increased by $37.9m and company tax rose by $28.3m – those results point to continued resilience in formal employment, wages, and business profitability.

The FRCS has also noted that fiscal duty, domestic excise duty, withholding tax and import excise duty recorded positive annual growth.

FRCS chief executive officer Udit Singh said the results demonstrated the resilience of the country’s economy despite geopolitical uncertainty, international fuel-supply pressures, imported inflation and softer expectations for tourism and consumer activity.

“This record result reflects the strength of Fiji’s underlying business and employment base,” Mr Singh said.

“Businesses continued to operate and contribute, employers-maintained jobs and wages, trade remained active, and taxpayers continued to support the country despite a challenging economic environment.”

Meanwhile, net VAT declined by $102.8m compared with the previous year, principally reflecting the reduction in the VAT rate from 15 per cent to 12.5 per cent, together with refund and payment-timing effects.

However, Mr Singh said the decline should not be interpreted as an equivalent reduction in underlying economic activity.

The July collection was $288.8m, which was $16.6m below forecast and $22.3m below July 2025.

Mr Singh said the softer monthly result was influenced by the timing of company income tax returns and higher refunds.

“Nevertheless, the strong performance over the preceding 11 months enabled FRCS to finish the year well above its annual forecast.

“We should view this achievement with confidence but not complacency.

“The economic risks remain real by the breath of the revenue result shows that Fiji enters the new financial year with a resilient economic and fiscal foundation.”

Mr Singh acknowledged the taxpayers, businesses, employers, importers and exports, customs brokers and tax agents.

“This achievement belongs first and foremost to Fiji’s taxpayers.

“Every dollar collected supports essential public services, including healthcare, education, infrastructure, social assistance and border protection.

“I also thank the FRCS board for its leadership and governance, our staff for their professionalism and commitment, and the Government, Ministry of Finance, Reserve Bank of Fiji and our partner agencies for their continued cooperation and support.”

item.title: Suva Open expands with new junior grades
item.description: THE fourth Vodafone Suva Open Tennis Tournament, set for August 21 to 24, will for the first time include Under-7, Under-8, and Under-10 divisions, expanding the competition beyond the existing Under-12, Under-14, and Under-16 categories. item.content:encoded:
THE fourth Vodafone Suva Open Tennis Tournament, set for August 21 to 24, will for the first time include Under-7, Under-8, and Under-10 divisions, expanding the competition beyond the existing Under-12, Under-14, and Under-16 categories.

The tournament, hosted at the Victoria and Paradiso tennis courts in Suva, reflects the Suva Tennis Association’s commitment to nurturing tennis at the grassroots level.

Vice-president Daniel Naidu highlighted that the new grades aim to open access to the sport for younger children, many of whom would not normally have tennis opportunities.

“We have a big tennis programme with schools, where close to 400 students regularly attend sessions at the Victoria Tennis Courts,” Naidu said.

He added that the association’s free coaching schools programme is a vital part of developing the next generation of players throughout Suva.

Since its inception, the tournament has grown significantly – from 91 player entries across 12 divisions in its inaugural year to a record 163 last year, marking an 80 percent increase.

It now draws competitors not only from Suva but also from across Fiji, Samoa, the Solomon Islands, and Australia.

Naidu noted the tournament’s rising importance as a regional event and a key preparation ground for major competitions like the Pacific Games.

He also acknowledged Vodafone’s ongoing support, which has been instrumental in enhancing participation and tennis development over the past three years.

This four-day event will showcase a wide age range of players, from the newly introduced youngest categories to seniors, promising exciting competition for local and international tennis enthusiasts.

item.title: Young star’s big moment
item.description: THE 2026 Commonwealth Games in Glasgow was more than just another international competition for 17-year-old sprinter Adi Ceva Lutumailagi. It was the fulfilment of a lifelong dream.
item.content:encoded:
THE 2026 Commonwealth Games in Glasgow was more than just another international competition for 17-year-old sprinter Adi Ceva Lutumailagi.

It was the fulfilment of a lifelong dream.

As the youngest member of Team Fiji, Lutumailagi embraced every moment of her maiden Commonwealth Games appearance, describing the experience as unforgettable despite the challenge of competing against some of the world’s best athletes.

“It was fun, surprising, and I really loved it,” she said.

The Nadi track star said simply qualifying for the Games was a personal victory as she always dreamed of competing on one of the biggest stages in international sport.

“The target was met. I finally made it to the Commonwealth Games. I’ve always dreamt of it and competing against athletes from countries like Canada, Jamaica, Scotland and England. It was an amazing experience.”

Lutumailagi said representing Fiji as the youngest athlete at another major international event was both an honour and a privilege.

“I have always been the youngest athlete going and competing in international games. I would say it’s an honour, and I’m so grateful. I’m still making my way, but I’m thankful to be there.”

She also acknowledged the unwavering support she received throughout her journey, expressing gratitude to her family, supporters and the Team Fiji contingent in Scotland.

“One big thank you to all my family and supporters who helped me in this journey with athletics, and to my other family who was with me in Scotland. Thank you for all the support, love and care. God bless you all.”

Lutumailagi encouraged aspiring young athletes to remain committed to their goals, saying success comes through consistency, faith and hard work.

“Stay consistent with training, keep pushing yourself and pray about it. Always put God first in everything, stay humble, get your family behind you and train hard.”

Although her Glasgow campaign marked the beginning of her Commonwealth Games journey, Lutumailagi has already shown the determination and maturity of an athlete eager to achieve even greater success in the years ahead.

item.title: Springboks W brace for massive challenge
item.description: SOUTH Africa Women assistant coach Franzel September says his side is expecting one of its toughest assignments in its Rugby World Cup preparations when it faces the Vodafone Fijiana XV today. Speaking yesterday during the team’s captain’s run, September said the visitors had identified Fiji as an important benchmark on their road to the 2029 Rugby World Cup and could not afford to underestimate t
item.content:encoded:
SOUTH Africa Women assistant coach Franzel September says his side is expecting one of its toughest assignments in its Rugby World Cup preparations when it faces the Vodafone Fijiana XV today.

Speaking yesterday during the team’s captain’s run, September said the visitors had identified Fiji as an important benchmark on their road to the 2029 Rugby World Cup and could not afford to underestimate the challenge of playing the Fijiana on home soil.

“We know Fiji is a different beast at home, so we expect that it’s going to be a massive challenge for us,” September said.

The South Africans arrived in Fiji earlier this week and quickly shifted their focus to rugby after a long journey.

“First of all, it’s a massive privilege and honour to be here. We’re so grateful for this opportunity. The hospitality of the Fijians has been awesome and they’ve made us feel really welcome,” he said.

“But on Sunday afternoon we got stuck into rugby because we know exactly why we’re here.”

The fixture is another key step in South Africa’s long-term World Cup build-up, with the coaching staff using the tour to test combinations and expose players to different styles of rugby.

September expects Fiji to challenge his side with its physicality, attacking flair and ability to build momentum through quick ball movement.

“If you allow the Fijians to play their game, they’re good with ball in hand, they’re good defensively as well and they kick a bit too, so we need to stop the momentum.

“We need to make sure we play in the right areas of the field.”

Rather than changing their approach, South Africa will rely on the strengths that have shaped its identity.

“We’re a set-piece team and we know exactly what we’re good at. We can’t come here thinking things will just happen. We are prepared to work for it.”

The Springbok Women has been forced into one late change, with Alichia Arries replacing the injured Eloise Webb after Tuesday’s training session.

Despite the setback, September said every member of the 26-player touring squad has an important role to play throughout the tour.

He also welcomed the opportunity to play in front of a large crowd during Fiji’s secondary schools rugby competition, saying the atmosphere would provide another valuable test for his players.

“Rugby unites us in South Africa. If we can bring that to Fiji as well, why not? It’s part of the bigger picture,” he said.

item.title: ‘Character’ first as Grammar targets Dean’s glory
item.description: SUVA Grammar School’s rise as a powerhouse in Fiji secondary schools’ rugby is driven by one core philosophy: character over talent. This approach has crafted not only championship-winning teams but also resilient, disciplined young men and women embodying the school’s proud “Lion Spirit”.
item.content:encoded:
SUVA Grammar School’s rise as a powerhouse in Fiji secondary schools’ rugby is driven by one core philosophy: character over talent.

This approach has crafted not only championship-winning teams but also resilient, disciplined young men and women embodying the school’s proud “Lion Spirit”.

Today, Suva Grammar will showcase this spirit with the school represented in all grades at Vodafone Dean’s and Weetbix Raluve quarter-finals which will take place at three different venues across the country.

The Nasese school’s recent success is remarkable.

Last season they clinched the Dean’s under-15 and under-16 national titles.

Their dominant under-16 team, now in the under-17 grade, aims for a fourth consecutive national crown after another strong southern zone campaign.

Despite their growing reputation, principal Iosefo Masivue insists rugby is about more than trophies.

“Rugby is used to build character for our young men and women,” he said.

“The rugby field and rugby training is just another type of classroom for us. It’s where students learn skills not taught in traditional classrooms — social skills, emotional intelligence, and moral values that build their character.”

“Our motto for rugby over the past few years now is character over talent,” Masivue added.

“We do not just rely on the talent of our rugby players because character is the thing that will take them far with their rugby talent.”

There is no pressure for the six teams to win their national quater-finals; success is measured by each student’s growth through rugby.

Yet, the values instilled naturally fuel a fierce competitive edge — the Lion Spirit — a champion’s mentality forged through character long before the final whistle.

item.title: Fijiana XV set for historic Bok test
item.description: HISTORY will be made at HFC Bank Stadium today when the Vodafone Fijiana XV host Springbok Women for the first time on Fijian soil in an international Test kicking off at 1pm. The match also marks the first outing for the new Fijiana XV coaching group and the opening fixture of a two-Test series against the Springbok Women. The second Test will be played next week at Churchill Park in Lautoka, giv
item.content:encoded:
HISTORY will be made at HFC Bank Stadium today when the Vodafone Fijiana XV host Springbok Women for the first time on Fijian soil in an international Test kicking off at 1pm.

The match also marks the first outing for the new Fijiana XV coaching group and the opening fixture of a two-Test series against the Springbok Women. The second Test will be played next week at Churchill Park in Lautoka, giving Fiji another opportunity to measure itself against one of the world’s leading women’s rugby nations.

Leading the side into the historic encounter is captain Kolora Lomani, who believes the occasion is another major step forward for women’s rugby in Fiji.

“We’re pretty excited,” Lomani said during Friday’s captain’s run.

“It’s a historical game for us. First time ever for us to host South Africa in Fiji, so we’re looking forward to it, and we’re expecting a hard game as well from the South African team.”

While the occasion is significant, Lomani knows her side cannot afford to be distracted once the whistle blows.

“We’re just focusing on the collision of the game. They’re a strong team and we’re not taking them lightly,” she said.

“The first 20 minutes of the game we have to come hard and not let them walk over us. We’re going to have to play hard and spread the ball out wide when we can.”

Today’s test is part of a festival of rugby alongside the Vodafone Deans competition, allowing hundreds of secondary school players to witness elite international women’s rugby firsthand.

Lomani believes the occasion will inspire the next generation.

“It’s a very good exposure for rugby here in Fiji. To see the young girls coming through and the boys playing before and after us, it’s a good experience to see what it’s like to be in this environment.”

The match will also see Adi Vani Buleki (wing) and Ruth Raketekete (inside centre) make their Fijiana XV debuts after earning starting spots through consistent performances.

“They’ve earned their spot to start,” Lomani said.

As the anticipation builds, the skipper has called on supporters to fill HFC Bank Stadium.

“To all our supporters, our friends and our family, we’d love to see you out in numbers, not just to watch us, but to support the Deans competition as well.”

For the Fijiana XV, today is about more than making history. It is an opportunity to showcase how far women’s rugby in Fiji has come while taking on one of the sport’s toughest international opponents on home soil.

item.title: NETBALL FIJI REVIVAL I Invitational event eyes annual status
item.description: THE Fiji Invitational Tournament has delivered four days of exciting netball action at the Vodafone Arena, drawing in a good number of crowds every day, funded by the Fiji National Sports Commission. Across the opening days, fans witnessed fast-paced contests between Crest Fiji Black, Crest Fiji Blue, NSW Fiji Davui and the Auckland Fiji Davui, highlighting the growth of netball and the value of h
item.content:encoded:
THE Fiji Invitational Tournament has delivered four days of exciting netball action at the Vodafone Arena, drawing in a good number of crowds every day, funded by the Fiji National Sports Commission.

Across the opening days, fans witnessed fast-paced contests between Crest Fiji Black, Crest Fiji Blue, NSW Fiji Davui and the Auckland Fiji Davui, highlighting the growth of netball and the value of hosting quality international competition on home soil.

The tournament also celebrates the return of well-known former national netball representatives, including Vilimaina Davu, who was part of the team that helped Fiji reach sixth place at the 1999 World Netball Championship in Christchurch before later representing the Silver Ferns from 2001 to 2006.

Netball Fiji also welcomes the return of former Fiji Pearls captain Matila Waqanidrola and Tuipulotu McLennan, a netball gold medalist at the 1995 South Pacific Games in Tahiti.

Another major milestone has been the growing support from partners.

The Fiji National Sports Commission’s backing has helped make the tournament possible, while Netball Fiji’s new broadcast media partnership with FBC has ensured matches reach audiences across the country and around the world.

With the tournament proving a success, Netball Fiji TOC Chairperson Vasiti Vugakoto has confirmed the Fiji Invitational is here to stay.

“The response to this year’s Fiji Invitational has been overwhelming, and we are excited to announce that it will now become an annual event on our netball calendar.” Vugakoto said.

She said the tournament had already attracted significant international attention.

“This year we’ve welcomed teams from Australia and New Zealand, but we’ve also received expressions of interest from teams and players as far as the United Kingdom and United States.

That tells us there is genuine interest in what Netball Fiji is building, and we’re committed to providing a quality competition that continues to attract international participation while creating opportunities for our local players.”

Vugakoto also mentioned that this tournament attracted former national netball players.

“It is great to see many of our former national players return home with overseas-based teams to bring the competition back to Fiji and help expose our local players to a higher level of competition.

The overseas-based players bring different styles of play in both attack and defence.

It is an overwhelming experience to see our former reps supporting Netball Fiji’s new vision and pathway to the international level,” she said.

As the competition comes to an end, the selectors now face the difficult task of narrowing the squad ahead of the Oceania World Cup Qualifiers at Tonga in September.

item.title: BA RUGBY I Sea levels and rugby costs – both rising
item.description: EVERYTHING’S going up. Not just fuel prices and sea levels, but it feels like everything around rugby is also increasing. By the time Ba Rugby has covered the players’ bus fares, food, medical, accommodation, match fees and coaching costs for the three provincial teams, the total rises above $10,000 per week.
item.content:encoded:
EVERYTHING’S going up. Not just fuel prices and sea levels, but it feels like everything around rugby is also increasing.

By the time Ba Rugby has covered the players’ bus fares, food, medical, accommodation, match fees and coaching costs for the three provincial teams, the total rises above $10,000 per week.

And that’s without uniforms and equipment.

“We are fighting hard to keep our costs down,” BRU secretary Gaby Kautoga said, “but at times it feels like a losing battle.

“The only thing we can do is to look for more income.”

Adding to these inflationary pressures are the added hosting costs implemented this season by Fiji Rugby to offset their own historical deficits in running the provincial tournaments.

Each host union must now pay for the match officials and match management team, a sum of around $2500 each week that was previously borne by the parent body.

“We understand the reasons why FRU made the changes, and we accept them,” Kautoga said.

“It’s just difficult with everything else also going up.”

The Vinod Patel Ba men’s team wanted to camp again this week as they prepared for Tailevu’s arrival today. But cost became an issue.

So, to the rescue came the Vanua — different villages each day helping out with the catering for the 35 hungry players.

“This past week, Togalevu, Sorokoba, Toge and Nailaga have taken it in turns to provide the main meals for the boys, even consulting with each other on the menus to get a variety of foods for the players.”

“Next week, Votua, Natalecake and Koronubu have confirmed that they’ll be doing the cooking,” Kautoga said.

It’s a great initiative where the vanua get to help the team hands on and witness the daily lives of the province’s top players.

“We are extremely grateful to the villages who have stepped forward to help the cause. Their support has also helped to lift the spirits of the boys after their narrow loss to Suva last week.”

“It won’t get any easier either,” he said.

“After this Tailevu game, we have five away matches in a row and that means no gate income to offset the costs.”

“All the provincial unions are in the same position. I think we’re all finding it really hard this season.”

For the three games against Tailevu today, the gates at 4R Stadium, Govind Park, open at 10am with tickets being a flat $10 for adults and $5 for children under 12.
